coordinates.note: Approximate only — Church Mountain Road rises north/northwest of Jasper city center. Update latitude and longitude with a GPS reading on-site for precise weather API queries.

elevation.basis: Jasper city center sits at ~1,467 ft; KJZP Pickens County Airport is 1,535 ft. Church Mountain Road ascends a named mountain above town. Blue Ridge foothills in this area commonly run 1,600–2,100 ft on named mountain roads. Midpoint estimate of 1,750 ft used for calculations.
elevation.verifyInstruction: Open any maps or GPS app, navigate to 282 Church Mountain Road, and read your elevation. Update estimated_ft and set confidence to 'confirmed'.

hardiness.elevationAdjustedZone: 7a (exposed ridges and mid-slope); 6b possible in confirmed frost pockets
hardiness.explanation: Pickens County is officially USDA Zone 7b. At an estimated elevation of ~1,750 ft — roughly 280 ft above the KJZP reference station — the standard environmental lapse rate (3.5–5.5°F per 1,000 ft) implies approximately 1–1.5°F cooler average winter minimum. This alone keeps you squarely in 7b on open mid-slope positions. However, cold-air drainage into draws and hollows can push low spots an additional 8–15°F colder on calm clear nights, briefly reaching Zone 6b conditions. Plant accordingly: assume 7b for exposed and mid-slope beds, assume 7a or colder for any low-lying or sheltered hollow plantings.
hardiness.coldAirDrainageEffect_F: 8–15°F colder in valley bottoms / hollows on calm clear nights vs. mid-slope

frostDates.source: NOAA 1991–2020 Climate Normals for Jasper GA, elevation-adjusted for estimated ~280 ft above KJZP

valleyFloor_KJZP.note: These are the official climate-normal dates for the Jasper/KJZP station (1,535 ft) — your baseline reference.

atPropertyElevation.note: Adjusted ~+7 days spring / -7 days fall for estimated ~280 ft additional elevation. Applies to open mid-slope planting positions. Add another 5–14 days to frost-safe date for any beds in frost pockets.

frostDates.frostPocketWarning: Any hollow, draw, or low-lying area where cold air pools on calm nights can experience frost 1–4 weeks earlier in fall and later in spring than the open mid-slope estimates above. If you have beds in these spots, treat them as Zone 6b.

climate.precipitationNotes: 57 in/yr at valley station. Orographic lift on mountain slopes typically adds 5–15% over the valley reading — Church Mountain property likely receives 60–65 in/yr. Well distributed year-round with slight spring peak (Mar–May). Afternoon convective thunderstorms common Jun–Aug.

temperature.extremeWinterLow_F: Rarely below 10°F at mid-slope; frost pockets may briefly reach 0–5°F in hard winters

humidity.summer: High — 70–90% RH June–September; afternoon humidity combined with heat creates ideal conditions for fungal disease (boxwood blight, powdery mildew, downy mildew). Prioritize air circulation in plantings.
humidity.fallWinter: Moderate — drier, lower humidity; best season for outdoor work and soil amendments

wind.summer: Light and variable; primarily SW; afternoon thunderstorm outflow can produce sudden strong gusts
wind.winter: NW to NE; cold Canadian air masses; exposed ridge positions get significant wind chill and evergreen desiccation
wind.iceStormRisk: Moderate — Pickens County sits in the Appalachian cold-air damming zone; 1–3 ice events per winter typical. Freezing rain more likely than heavy snow.
wind.snowfall_in_avg: 5–12 inches annually; rarely accumulates more than 3–4 inches; melts quickly

climate.growingSeasonNotes: Warm enough for a long productive growing season, but late spring frosts mean wait until late May to plant tender annuals at elevation. Fall harvest window closes earlier than metro Atlanta by 2–3 weeks.

soils.parentMaterial: Residuum weathered from high-grade metamorphic and igneous rock — mica gneiss, mica schist, granodiorite. Typical of the Southern Appalachian Blue Ridge.
soils.texture: Sandy loam to loam surface horizon (A/E); red-yellow sandy clay loam to clay loam subsoil (Bt argillic horizon). Moderately high clay content in subsoil can impede drainage in flat areas.
soils.structure: Moderate granular structure when in good health; can become compacted and crusting when depleted of organic matter or heavily trafficked.

plantingTargets.acidLovers: 4.5–5.5 — azaleas, rhododendrons, mountain laurel, blueberries; your native soil is ideal unlimed
plantingTargets.generalShrubsAndTrees: 5.5–6.5 — dogwood, hydrangea, boxwood, holly, Japanese maple; may need light liming
plantingTargets.vegetables: 6.0–6.8 — may need liming for vegetable gardens
plantingTargets.turf: 6.0–6.5 — likely needs liming if establishing lawn areas

pH.soilTestRecommendation: Get a UGA Extension soil test for each distinct planting area before adding any amendments. $9 basic test through Pickens County Extension Office (706-253-8840). Tests for pH, P, K, Ca, Mg and give lime/fertilizer recommendations.

drainage.onSlopes: Well-drained to excessively drained — water moves through quickly; drought stress risk in summer
drainage.flatAreas: Watch for perched water tables above clay subsoil; test drainage by digging 12-inch hole and observing after rain
drainage.lowAreas: Potential for seasonal wet spots — check before planting moisture-sensitive species

organicMatter.native: Low to moderate on slopes; naturally depleted by erosion and rapid decomposition in warm humid climate
organicMatter.improvement: Annual additions of leaf mulch and compost are the single highest-return investment for mountain garden soil. 2–3 inch mulch layer year-round on all beds.

nutrients.potassium: Moderate to high from mica weathering — K deficiency uncommon
nutrients.phosphorus: Often low-to-medium; acidic soils fix P in unavailable forms. Test before adding P fertilizer.
nutrients.calcium_magnesium: Often low due to acidity; liming with dolomitic limestone raises pH and simultaneously adds Ca and Mg
nutrients.nitrogen: Low; organic matter additions and slow-release fertilizers most appropriate

soils.rockContent: Moderate to high — mica schist and gneiss parent material means rocks, chert, and occasionally large boulders near the surface. Raised beds may be preferable for intensive vegetable gardening.

microclimate.overview: Church Mountain Road sits in a highly variable microclimate zone. The combination of elevation, slope aspect, and topographic position (ridge vs. draw vs. mid-slope vs. valley bottom) can create temperature differences of 15–20°F across a single property on a calm clear night. Knowing your specific positions is more valuable than any regional average.
microclimate.elevationEffect: Every 500 ft above Jasper valley adds approximately 1.75–2.75°F cooler average temperature. Spring green-up 5–10 days later than downtown Jasper; fall color 1–2 weeks earlier.

south_southwest.bestFor: Heat-loving vegetables, sun-tolerant ornamentals, fruit trees
south_southwest.caution: High summer heat stress — water demands elevated; Japanese maple and azalea leaf scorch more likely here

north_northeast.bestFor: Azaleas, rhododendrons, mountain laurel, ferns, wildflowers, hostas
north_northeast.caution: Frost lingers later in spring; fungal disease (anthracnose, root rot) elevated by persistent moisture and shade

east.character: Morning sun, afternoon shade — the balanced optimum
east.bestFor: Hydrangeas, dogwoods, most ornamentals; broadest compatible plant list
east.caution: None significant — generally most favorable orientation for the plant list you have

west.caution: High afternoon water stress in summer; wind exposure from prevailing SW summer breezes

thermalBelt.description: Mid-slope positions approximately 100–400 ft above the valley floor are typically the frost-safest positions on any mountain property. Cold air, being denser than warm air, drains downhill on calm clear nights and pools in the valley while the mid-slope stays warmer.
thermalBelt.estimatedAdvantage_F: 3–8°F warmer than valley bottom on calm clear nights
thermalBelt.implication: Your best beds for borderline-hardy plants are on the middle slope, not the valley bottom or the exposed ridge top.

frostPockets.description: Any topographic low — hollow, draw, depression, base of a slope, area surrounded by tree walls that block drainage — is a frost pocket. Cold air pools there on calm clear nights.
frostPockets.identification: On a clear calm night in spring or fall, use a thermometer to compare your low spots vs. mid-slope. A 10°F difference is not uncommon.
frostPockets.gardeningImplication: Do not plant marginally-hardy species in known frost pockets. Good uses for frost pockets: native woodland species, hardy ferns, cold-tolerant vegetables.

orographicPrecipitation.description: Moist air flowing up the mountain slopes cools and drops moisture as it rises — orographic lift. Church Mountain likely receives 5–15% more rainfall than the KJZP valley station records.
orographicPrecipitation.implication: Drainage is important; hillside beds drain quickly but lower/flat areas may stay wetter than expected. Summer dry spells still happen — they just may be shorter than in the valley.
